scenes.title:
Build Your First [[AI Agent]]
in Java
scenes.subtitle: LLM + tools + a loop, with the official Anthropic Java SDK

lines.say: Everyone talks about AI agents. But if you're a Java developer, most tutorials are in Python.
Today, you'll build your first agent in plain Java, with the official Anthropic SDK.
No framework, no magic. About a hundred lines you'll understand completely.

scenes.heading: What is an [[agent]]?
items: An **LLM**: Claude, the brain that reads and decides
**Tools**: Java methods Claude can ask you to run
A **loop**: keep going until Claude has its answer

lines.say: So, what is an agent?
An agent is three things. First, a large language model. Here, Claude. It reads, thinks, and decides.
Second, tools. Normal Java methods that Claude is allowed to ask for.
And third, a loop. Your program keeps talking to Claude until the job is done.
Think of Claude as a smart manager with no hands. It decides what to do. Your code does it.

rows.label: You send
rows.text: The question, plus the list of tools

rows.label: You run the tool
rows.text: Send the result back, then ask again

lines.say: Here's how the loop works.
One: you send Claude the question, plus a list of the tools it may use.
Two: Claude either answers, or replies with stop reason, tool use. That means: please run this tool for me.
lines.tts: Two: Claude either answers, or replies with stop reason: tool use. That means: please run this tool for me.

lines.say: Three: your Java code runs the tool, and sends the result back.
Then you ask again. You repeat while the stop reason is tool use. That's the whole agent.

left.title: Build an agent when…
left.body:
• Claude needs live data:
  time, files, your database

right.title: A single call is enough when…
right.body:

• Nothing to look up
  or execute

lines.say: When should you build an agent?
When Claude needs live data, like the time or your database. When it must act. Or when the steps aren't known in advance.
If Claude can answer from text alone, like a summary or a translation, one simple call is enough. Start simple.

left.title: Plain chatbot
left.body:
"What time is it?"

Claude can't see your clock.
It can only say it doesn't know.

Big math? It might
get a digit wrong.

right.title: Our agent
right.body:
get_current_time → your clock
calculate → exact Java math

Claude combines both
into one clear answer

✓ Real data, exact numbers

lines.say: Our use case is small on purpose: a helper that knows the time, and does exact math.
A plain chatbot can't see your computer's clock. And with big numbers, it's better to compute than to guess.
Our agent gets two tools: one reads the clock, one does the math in Java. Claude decides when to use each.
Here's a plain chatbot first. One question, one answer, no tools.
I ask Claude what time it is.

do.match: What time is it right now?
do.label: Just a question

lines.say: Claude answers that it can't see the current time. It's honest, but not helpful. Let's fix that with an agent.

out: Claude: I don't have access to a clock, so I
can't tell you the current time.

lines.say: Step one: add the Anthropic Java SDK.

do.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>agent</groupId>
    <artifactId>java-first-agent</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- The official Anthropic Java SDK -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.anthropic</groupId>
            <artifactId>anthropic-java</artifactId>
            <version>2.71.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Lets us run the agent with: mvn compile exec:java -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>agent.MyFirstAgent</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

lines.say: It's a normal Maven project. The only dependency is anthropic java, the official SDK.
lines.tts: It's a normal Maven project. The only dependency is anthropic-java, the official S D K.

lines.say: And the exec plugin lets us run the agent with one Maven command.
The SDK reads your API key from an environment variable, called ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Never put the key in your code.
lines.tts: The S D K reads your A P I key from an environment variable, called anthropic underscore A P I underscore key. Never put the key in your code.

lines.say: Step two: write the tools. I create a class called Tools.
A tool is just a Java method. This one returns the current date and time. This one does exact math on two numbers.
Notice they return text. Claude reads the result as text, even errors like divide by zero.
Claude never runs these methods itself. It can only ask. Your program runs them.
Step three: describe the tools to Claude.
Each tool gets a name, a description, and an input schema: the inputs it takes.

do.text:
// 2. Descriptions Claude reads to decide WHEN to use a tool
    static final Tool TIME = Tool.builder()
            .name("get_current_time")
            .description("Returns the current local date and time. "
                    + "Use it for any question about now or today.")
            .inputSchema(Tool.InputSchema.builder()
                .properties(Tool.InputSchema.Properties.builder()
                    .build())
                .build())
            .build();

    static final Tool CALCULATOR = Tool.builder()
            .name("calculate")
            .description("Does exact math on two numbers. "
                    + "Use it for any arithmetic.")
            .inputSchema(Tool.InputSchema.builder()
                .properties(Tool.InputSchema.Properties.builder()
                    .putAdditionalProperty("op", JsonValue.from(Map.of(
                        "type", "string",
                        "enum", List.of("add", "subtract",
                                        "multiply", "divide"))))
                    .putAdditionalProperty("a", JsonValue.from(
                        Map.of("type", "number")))
                    .putAdditionalProperty("b", JsonValue.from(
                        Map.of("type", "number")))
                    .build())
                .required(List.of("op", "a", "b"))
                .build())
            .build();

lines.say: The calculator takes an operation, and two numbers, a and b. All three are required.
The description is the most important part. Claude reads it to decide when to use the tool. So say what it does, and when to use it.
Step four: when Claude asks for a tool, we need to run the right method.
The run method takes Claude's tool call, reads its inputs, and picks the method by name.
Claude sends the inputs as JSON. I convert them to a map, then call calculate with the operation and the numbers.
lines.tts: Claude sends the inputs as Jason. I convert them to a map, then call calculate with the operation and the numbers.

lines.say: An unknown tool name returns an error message, instead of crashing.
Step five, the heart of every agent: the loop. I create MyFirstAgent.
First, the client, which reads the API key. Then I read the user's question.
lines.tts: First, the client, which reads the A P I key. Then I read the user's question.

lines.say: The builder holds the whole conversation: the model, Claude Opus five point five, the two tools, and the question.
Now the loop. I send the conversation, and save Claude's reply in the history. Then I print any text Claude wrote.
This matters: Claude has no memory between calls. We send the full history every time.
Next, the exit. If the stop reason isn't tool use, Claude is done, so we break out of the loop.
Otherwise, I run every tool Claude asked for, and collect the results.
Then I send all the results back together, in one message. Each result carries the id of the call it answers.
lines.tts: Then I send all the results back together, in one message. Each result carries the I D of the call it answers.

lines.say: Then the loop starts again, and Claude sees the results.
Time to test. First, an offline check of the tools. No API key needed.
lines.tts: Time to test. First, an offline check of the tools. No A P I key needed.

lines.say: Both tools work, and the errors come back as text. Now the real agent.
I ask: what time is it, and what is twelve thirty four times fifty six seventy eight?

out: Ask your agent: What time is it, and what is

lines.say: Claude asked for both tools. Our Java code ran them, and sent back the results.
Then Claude used the real time and the exact number in one clear answer. That's your first agent.

cards.title: Describe tools well
cards.text: What it does, and when to use it

cards.title: Return errors as text
cards.text: Claude can read them and recover

cards.title: Limit the loop
cards.text: Add a max number of turns

cards.title: Keep tools small
cards.text: One job per tool, clear inputs

lines.say: Four tips for your next agent.
One: write clear tool descriptions. They decide when Claude uses each tool.
Two: return errors as text, instead of throwing. Claude reads them, and can try again.
Three: limit the loop. In a real app, stop after a maximum number of turns, so it can never run forever.
And four: keep each tool small, with one job and clear inputs.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: Tools are Java methods; Claude **asks**, your code **runs** them
Loop while `stop_reason` is [[TOOL_USE]], and keep the history

lines.say: Let's recap.
An agent is an LLM, plus tools, plus a loop.
Tools are plain Java methods. Claude asks, your code runs them.
And the loop continues while the stop reason is tool use, sending the full history every time.
